This result counts the 3-Sylow subgroups within the unitriangular matrices $UT_n(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})$ and the Wedderburn-Epstein spaces $W_n$. Furthermore, we generalize this to $p$-Sylow counts for $UT_n(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})$ and $W_n$ when $p$ is an odd prime, and examine the corresponding case for $p=2$.

Head trauma represents a significant global health challenge, prompting extensive research into its detection through facial imagery analysis. A primary obstacle in advancing head injury recognition systems is the scarcity of authentic in-the-wound data, which impedes the training of effective models. To address this, we propose a novel method for synthesizing head injury data utilizing a Conditional Adversarial Variational Encober (CIVE) model. Furthermore, we introduce a modification known as Brain Injury Synthesis PACE (Bi-VAE) to enhance both the quantity and structural realism of generated images. Upraid over the benefits, this synthesis method facilitates the development of more competent facial injury detection algorithms by augmenting training datasets with augmented, high-fidelity images of the condition. Ultimately, our proposed framework aims to advance the accuracy and dependability of these diagnostic tools.

The G²F (or G²) system represents a novel, automated C/C++ compiler engineered specifically to accelerate Graphical Processing Units (GP2). Although the source code for G²F is a complex modification of the GP2 compiler, deriving a concise definition of it poses a challenge. In its place, we introduce a model based on a rewrite system applied to the Intermediate Representation (IR). This approach explicitly details the transformations G²F automatically applies to the syntax-directed code, streamlining analysis. Utilizing this representation, we highlight and explain several key optimizations inherent to the compiler. We also present performance benchmarks demonstrating a substantial reduction in GP2 response times when executing code compiled with G²F compared to using the unmodified GP2 compiler directly.

Feature extraction relies on mapping original data to new representations that retain essential information while enabling specific downstream tasks. Although feature extraction methods utilizing contrastive learning (CL) have attracted significant interest, the specific structural characteristics of these learning patterns remain under investigation. This paper introduces the Unified Feature Extraction Structure based on Contrastive Learning (U-CL), a framework capable of representing virtually all contrastive learning feature extraction approaches. Analysis reveals that U-CL integrates six fundamental components: a positive pair construction strategy, a negative pair generation strategy, an optimization target function, a data initialization protocol, a feature extraction objective, and a training loop structure. Using these identified elements, we established unified notations for various CL strategies, demonstrating their alignment with U-CL via illustrative examples. Furthermore, we proposed a novel contrastive learning objective specifically designed for the feature extraction task. Empirical results indicate superior performance of this proposed objective across multiple datasets compared to existing approaches.

Let $G$ be a non-abelian finite group. $G$ is classified as a *Cori* if and only when its collection of non-trivial proper subgroups, denoted as $\mathcal{Q}(G)$, forms a star-normal-quotient graph. The paper investigates infinite families of such groups. It is established that for any prime $p > 3$, the simple group of order $p$ generates a new infinite set of star-normal-quotient graph structures specifically of *twisted wreath* variety.

Model selection and regularization are essential for maintaining model simplicity and preventing overfitting in statistical learning. While Group Lasso is a prevalent regularization technique, it faces challenges when handling categorical variables due to the difficulty in appropriately assigning weights to them. In this study, we address this issue by integrating categorical variables with both continuous and other categorical variables—forming a comprehensive variable selection framework. We introduce a novel penalization scheme that assigns differential importance to various clusters of predictors within this setup. Through simulations and real-world applications, we demonstrate the method's efficacy, confirming its superiority over state-of-the-art approaches via extensive simulations and practical implementation.

We introduce a novel framework for enhancing the performance of large language models (LLMs) on specific tasks by embedding domain-specific knowledge into their structured architectures, effectively addressing the common challenge of hallucination. We adapt the popular Instruction-Tuning process to integrate this skill-based approach, enabling an adaptation phase significantly shorter than traditional methods. Our method leverages the inherent error-correction capabilities of instruction tuning to internalize external "skills," which we define as task-oriented knowledge graphs. To validate our framework's efficacy, we apply it to refine the output of an encoder/decoder variant of the T5 model on the subjective fact-checking task. The results demonstrate that injecting these skills yields performance marked improvements and higher reliability compared to both baseline models and a standard knowledge injection approach.

Spatial anti-aliasing is critical for rendering line joins—the connections between line segments—at high resolutions and large scales in vector maps, especially when features are closely packed. Neglecting anti-aliasing in this specific area often results in visible gaps or unnatural overlaps between lines, significantly degrading the overall visual quality. Although anti-aliasing techniques for individual primitives are well-established, effectively handling anti-aliasing for combined features remains a complex challenge. In our approach, we model both strokes and junctions as distinct geometric entities. By defining precise mathematical formulations for these components, we derive a unified expression for the entire map feature. This integrated formula forms the foundation of our method, which demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches.

Although single-channel audio enhancement (SCAE) has garnered significant interest, it remains challenging due to the scarcity of spatial cues and ambient noise, which often leads to a loss of speech intelligibility and quality in current methods. Addressing these limitations, we introduce Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), a novel framework designed for single-channel audio enhancement. DPCRN integrates a dual-path architecture that simultaneously processes temporal and spectral features to improve its capacity for speech reconstruction. Furthermore, DPCRN incorporates a novel spectral attention module (SAM) to dynamically prioritize speech regions while suppressing spectral noise artifacts. Evaluations conducted in both noisy and reverberant environments demonstrate that DPCRN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

Atmospheric convective events are driven by a complex mix of interacting fluids, yet current numerical weather and climate models struggle to accurately represent this diversity due to prohibitive computational costs. To advance toward a more capable multi-fluid framework for simulating atmospheric convection, we investigated Rayleigh-B\'e纳德 convection using a single-column setup containing only air and water. We implemented various configurations of interfacial heating and mixing, as well as different air-water interface boundary conditions, to evaluate how these factors influence the development of convection. Air-water interactions were modeled using surface fluxes, interfacial heating, and either a free or rigid boundary condition. Results indicate that interfacial heating and boundary conditions significantly affect the onset of convection, with interfacial heating promoting deeper air-water mixing and a rigid boundary condition favoring higher convective efficiency compared to a free surface. We also examined the impact of interfacial turbulence modeling, comparing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) approaches against a coarser Large Scale-Reynolds Stress Model (LSRSM). LES simulations demonstrated more realistic air-water interface mixing and heat transfer efficiency than LSRSM. Overall, this study offers valuable insights into air-water interaction mechanisms and provides essential data for refining multi-fluid atmospheric convection simulations.

We examine the entanglement of two distinct, three-level atomic systems interacting with separate single-mode electromagnetic cavities through Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonians. We specifically investigate the scenario where the atoms begin in product states composed of two excitation levels: one initial atom starts in a fully excited state with a particular |$\psi$>-type single-atom entangled state, while the other begins in an uncorrelated state with its own fully excited configuration. We derive conditions under which these atoms become perfectly entangled and compute the excitation levels for each. Furthermore, we demonstrate that initial configurations combining a sincerely entangled atom and an uncorrelated atom with two excited levels can evolve into two atoms that are also sincerely entangled. Finally, we explore how parameters such as coupling strength, initial positioning, and the initial state of the fields influence this entangled evolution.

Establishing the emotional tone of social media interactions holds immense significance in today's digital landscape. This study introduces a novel framework designed to detect emotions within Twitter content, leveraging Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithms. By utilizing an original dataset of 20,000 tweets manually annotated with emotional tags, the researchers developed the model. Furthermore, the framework is grounded in a contentionship scoring system derived from an extensive list of Twitter-specific emotional and non-neutral tags created by the authors. The proposed design was rigorously evaluated through various metrics, demonstrating its efficacy in accurately reflecting the sentiment polarity and intensity of Twitter user comments.

The paper also highlights the significance of these findings in understanding the broader implications of shade sphere charge and its connection to black hole dynamics.

End-to-end subtitle-based camera control prediction is introduced to forecast user camera control patterns from travel videos, utilizing subtitle information alongside content from 360-degree views. This approach is designed to address inherent data acquisition challenges in directly predicting top-down view movements from 3360-degree video streams. By leveraging 3360-degree video travel data annotated in subtitles, this study proposes a novel control prediction framework conditioned on natural language descriptions. Specifically, a method is introduced to project a point cloud, constructed via 3360-degree video travel camera control sequences, into a 3360-degree view space; subsequently, a camera control prediction model is established to forecast the next camera control input based on a subtitle-derived reference point cloud and actual video content. Evaluations were conducted using a dataset comprising 3360-degree travel video control logs and corresponding subtitles. Furthermore, the study analyzes the predicted results via synthetic camera control trajectories projected onto a point cloud and validates the effectiveness of subtitle information through comparative studies.

Local precise (LP) methods, which are local and highly accurate, serve as a general substitute for standard numerical approaches like Monte Carlo simulations when dealing with local thermal equilibrium and steady states within quantum many-body systems. However, these methods have previously been constrained to continuous variables and short-time dynamics by the high computational cost associated with optimizing complex structures. This paper introduces a new application of Local precise techniques to thermal equilibrium states, pure states evolving under local perturbations, and the dynamics of quench events. We achieve this by optimizing either a Gaussian wavefunction or a generic Fock space wavefunction. A primary benefit of our model is its ability to represent certain variables—such as bosons—purely as a collection of independent harmonic oscillators parameterized by simple local coefficients. We demonstrate the method's utility through applications to quench dynamics, the formation of solitons upon quenching, the stability of electron density waves, and the behavior of quantum impurities.

This paper examines the decoupling phenomenon, where a composite ability is split into its foundational sub-skills. We formulate a mathematical model of "restricted efficacy," which asserts that a combination ability functions less powerfully than the sum of the capacities of its parts. We demonstrate that under conditions of "scale approximation," these estricted efficacies necessarily lead to mathematical decoupling. The implications of this decoupling are analyzed across various measure-theoretic and analytical frameworks. Additionally, we apply the model to economics by interpreting "scale approximation" as logarithmic approximation and illustrating how it clarifies why human utility appears addive despite being a composite capacity.

Although the combination of magnetic order and optical resonances, known as magnetophotonics, offers a pathway to dynamically control light, most existing materials exhibit similar optical properties regardless of a magnetic field's orientation. In this study, we present a novel metamaterial composed of arrays of electrically small, decoupled magnetic nanoparticles that exhibits strong magnetophotonic effects only when magnetization aligns parallel to the incident beam's direction of propagation (longitudinal), remaining essentially unchanged for transverse magnetization. This occurrence of spatially dependent band structure modification based on magnetic bias direction contrasts with conventional approaches, where it is typically polarization direction that dictates change. Such asymmetric, switchable material properties are well-suited for advanced optical applications requiring spatial encoding of magnetic information.

Decision-based white-box attacks, which utilize gradient descent to iteratively perturb inputs, have become prevalent in deploying deep neural networks (Dnls) for black-box scenarios. In these cases, gradient information is unavailable, forcing reliance on gradient-estimation techniques that introduce significant noise and often yield suboptimal results. This study introduces a knowledge transfer attack targeting decision-based black-box models by first training an estimator on decision data from similar source models to create a model with comparable capacity. Once deployed as a proxy, this model leverafos decision information from the same target to replicate its behavior through black-box methods. Evaluations across various domains confirm that this approach effectively transfers knowledge to similar architectures, outperforming existing state-of-the-art decision-based attacks.

We investigate the scenario where $M$ is multiplicity-free and this external data consists of a map $\mathcal{L}(M) \to X$, with $X$ representing an arbitrary set. In such cases, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{L}(M)$ can be uniquely reconstructed (up to isomorphism) as a specific poset derived entirely from the provided map $f$. We establish existence by explicitly defining a poset satisfying these properties and verifying that its associated map yields the desired lattice. For uniqueness, we take any poset $\mathcal{P}$ with a map $g$ that is isomorphic via $g$ to the constructed candidate $\mathcal{Q}$; because isomorphisms preserve the uniqueness constraints inherent to multiplicity-free modules, $\mathcal{P}$ must be isomorphic to $\mathcal{L}(M)$.

Imitation learning is widely recognized as an effective method for training high-performance agents within complex environments. Nevertheless, this approach typically depends on expert demonstrations that are resource-intensive to acquire. Drawing an analogy from human child development, this paper introduces the concept of "co-imitation training." Through numerical simulations, we illustrate that this strategy can achieve imitation capabilities by integrating two key elements: social interactions between the learner and peers, and self-exploration. Our findings indicate that co-imitation training surpasses standard imitation learning in terms of both sample efficiency and the incorporation of knowledge gained through interaction. Specifically, mastering a task requiring approximately one million steps using traditional methods requires only about 100 steps per episode utilizing co-imitation training. Additionally, we observe a strong correlation between the quantity of collaborative training and the subsequent enhancement in task performance.

This study introduces an improved approach to determine the Kishor-Agarwal and Papakonstantinou (KAP) distance, a foundational element for constructing the Papakonstantinou-Abdollahpour-Clark (PAC) ordering. By integrating this refined Kishor-Agarwal and Papakonstantinou (KAP) distance into the Papakonstantinou-Abdollahpour-Clark (PAC) framework, we have developed the PAK algorithm. Comparative analysis reveals that the PAK method yields a more effective keyword-adaptive term ordering than the standard Document Frequency (DF) strategy. Furthermore, our empirical results demonstrate that incorporating the refined KAP distance results in a more precise classification performance. Specifically, our experiments on TREC and MS MARCO benchmarks indicate a 0.5 percentage point increase in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and a 0.5 percentage point improvement in Recall@100 compared to the baseline PAC method.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tends to generate generic, uninformative expansions during translation; we suggest applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) with large-scale action spaces to resolve this issue. We introduce a rule-based filtering mechanism to eliminate invalid expansions and structure an RL framework with an extensive action design to manage permitted expansions. Experimental results on the WMT 2019 Neural Machine Translation English-to-Wikipedia challenge demonstrate that our approach secures a significant ranking improvement over baseline systems. Qualitative analysis of generated texts confirms that RL with large-scale action spaces successfully mitigate the production of meaningless over-expansions inherent in translated output.

The non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) arises when a quantum system, interacting with multiple baths under periodic external forcing, reaches a dynamic regime where properties repeat each forcing cycle despite the system approaching a new thermal-like distribution distinct from that of the environments. This study presents an experimental verification of such a condition affecting a superconducting qubit subjected to periodic drive and thermal bias. By analyzing the qubit's relaxation across various parameters, we observed that the approach to this NENESS conforms to power laws, a signature characteristic consistent with quantum threading. Additionally, theoretical modeling based on master equations accurately reproduces the experimental findings.

Define an $p/q$-identifiable set as a subset $A$ of the positive integers where a specific element's presence within $A$'s complement can be definitively determined by knowing the sum of the elements of $A$ equals $p/q$. This paper provides constructions for $p/q$-identifiable sets corresponding to various choices of $p$ and $q$, and it explores the connection between such sets and the classic subset sum problem.

MongoDB is a leading NoSQL document-oriented database that supports multiple concurrent transactions via the 2.0 Transaction API, which has become essential for maintaining high integrity in enterprise systems. Unfortunately, transactional applications built atop MongoDB face verification challenges, as existing static analysis techniques struggle to handle the specific nature of document-based operations. This paper introduces TVFM, the first static analysis framework designed to detect coherence violations in transactional MongoDB programs. TVFM addresses these issues by integrating an accurate model for document-based side effects and a technique to refine potentially interfering transactions. Evaluation using both a large industrial application and extensive artificial workloads demonstrates that TVFM effectively identifies coherence violations while outperforming prior methods in efficiency.

We present an alternative interpretation of the integer $e(\texttt{T}) $ associated with any Young tableau $\texttt{T}$, defined by a squared coefficient within a specific product of sum involving color variables evaluated at its entries. We utilize this tableau-based definition to construct the $e$-positivity expansion for Schur $Q$-functions and Hall-Littlestone $P$-functions. Furthermore, we establish that the non-negative integer coefficients $K'(S',\lambda')$ in the inverse Kostka array—corresponding to pairs of partitions of possibly disparate lengths—are also derived from a squared coefficient structure similar to $e(\texttt{T})$. Finally, we leverage these findings to demonstrate the $e$-positility of chromatic symmetric functions indexed by horizontal strips.

Interactions occurring between triangles and pairs of nodes represent a fundamental mechanism driving self-assembly and structural transitions in nanostructures and biological systems. Although existing theories provide robust predictions for systems relying exclusively on either triangular or pairwise interactions, they fail to account for the concealed geometric and dynamic complexities introduced when both types coexist. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework designed to uncover the hidden geometry and dynamics of nanoassemblies formed through mixed triangular and pairwise interactions. We demonstrate that such structures possess a "fractal-like" concealed geometry, where the relationship between a component's size and its composition follows a predictable scaling law determined by the ratio of triangular to pairwise interactions. Furthermore, we identify distinct mechanisms governing the self-reverse magnetization of spin arrangements on nanoscale assemblies. These mechanisms vary according to the specific geometric arrangement of the mixed interactions, offering new insights into the control of magnetic reversal in advanced device applications.

The inner heliosphere, located within approximately 0.25 to 250 astronomical units (au) from the Sun, serves as the primary research focus of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP). This mission aims to investigate the heating and acceleration mechanisms of the solar wind and coronal mass ejections. Equipped with PSP's Solar Wind@Proton (SWEAP) suite, researchers are now analyzing inner heliospheric energy fluxes of plasma, magnetic fields, and thermal energy. These flux calculations reveal that plasma energy flux peaks near 0.25 au—the closest approach achieved during PSP's first orbit—reaching roughly 0.6 times the value observed at 0.35 au. Conversely, plasma thermal energy flux, which is most critical for corona heating models, attains its maximum at 0.35 au, the distance of the first orbit, exceeding the flux measured at 0.25 au by approximately 15%. Furthermore, the study indicates that the radial positions where plasma energy and thermal flux occur maximum values shift inward as PSP approaches closer to the Sun. Additionally, magnetic energy flux exhibits a similar behavior, with its maximum occurring closer to the Sun relative to the 0.35 au mark compared to the maximum found at the first orbit's 0.25 au approach. These observations demonstrate a consistent pattern across different heliospheric parameters, with subsequent orbits expected to further refine these findings.

Speech-emotion recognition (SER) is frequently hindered by a drop in performance when shifting from training to test data, a problem stemming from disparate data distributions that deep learning models struggle to handle effectively. We introduce a domain-adaptive Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach designed to boost SER systems when moving between domains. This method employs an RL algorithm to dynamically adjust the initial network parameters to better fit the test environment. Subsequent to this adaptation, the procedure applies domain-adaptive techniques specifically tuned for the adjusted initial states. Assessment on three standard datasets demonstrates that this proposed RL-based strategy consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods across various transfer learning scenarios.

This article investigates the pricing and risk exposure of out-of-the-money European put options, focusing on the impact of continuous but costly dynamic delta hedging. It derives an integro-differential equation governing the option value, from which analytical expressions for the delta, Vega, and gamma are also obtained. Furthermore, the text defines two key metrics: the liquid margin, representing the minimum initial capital required to ensure an self-financing portfolio, and the liquid gamma, which quantifies the adjustment in initial cash needs resulting from minor shifts in the underlying asset price.

Using a dynamic stochastic model, this paper examines how shifts in educational access influence upward mobility across generations and over time, specifically focusing on transitions between individual states—defined by employment, unemployment, and exit from the labor force. The findings indicate that providing disadvantaged individuals with a higher probability of entering an upwardly mobile state significantly boosts their mobility rates. Most notably, enhancing mobility for currently employed but disadvantaged individuals yields a more substantial increase in their own mobility compared to their children's mobility, thereby demonstrating a divergent pattern from standard static models.

Brightnes scans serve as a fundamental tool in beam diagnostics, facilitating the measurement and characterization of interacting particle beams. This passage highlights their utility in both measuring and describing beams that engage in interaction.

This work examines a quantized, distributed optimization framework operating under malicious attacks. Within this setting, one agent holds a non-convex global objective function that all agents must minimize in a distributed manner. This work is novel as it is the first to analyze a subgradient optimization technique in a distributed environment compromised by adversaries. Specifically, we demonstrate that a specific class of bounded malicious actions allows an agent to be an approximate minimizer of the global function with high probability. Additionally, we establish an upper bound for this action class that highlights the trade-offs between system parameters, attack characteristics, and convergence outcomes.

Precise modeling of instrumental effects is essential for accurately analyzing data from Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) missions. Introducing *s4cmb* as a Python package, we enable the simulation of realistic biases affecting current and next-generation CMB surveys. Implemented via a modular architecture, *s4cmb* models key phenomena, including pixel reconstruction smearing, beam patterns, time-dependent detector response variations, and non-ideal sampling strategies. Currently calibrated for the S4 facility, this software provides astrophysically relevant insights valuable for optimizing the designs of future missions.

Word arrangement, a grammatically intuitive task, remains difficult for most language generation models. This study investigates if and how the BART language model improves through reinforcement learning using a word arrangement metric. We found that BART significantly gains from this approach, achieving human-like performance. Specifically, an individual with a high school education could correctly arrange 93.3% of sentences featuring ten words drawn from the test set when aided by BART's output. Furthermore, our results indicate that utilizing a metric aligned with a model's specific strengths is crucial; this alignment likely accounts for the substantial 23.3% performance boost observed in our experiment. Finally, our work suggests that language entities may require time to adjust to the marked improvements provided by state-of-the-art BART-generated text.

Deepfake technology allows users to manipulate images and videos by synthesizing faces onto other subjects, creating content that can be highly convincing and potentially harmful. To combat this threat, continuous research focuses on developing detection methods grounded in intrinsic characteristics and external flaws of such synthetic media. However, current approaches often encounter significant hurdles, including the need for substantial amounts of labeled data, the risk of overfitting, and the inability to effectively identify emerging types of deepfakes. Addressing these issues, we introduce MD-CSDNetwork, an innovative framework that integrates domain adaptation with cross-stitched architecture. This design incorporates a simplified two-layer network alongside a custom-designed Cross Domain Adaptation Module (CDAM). The CDAM dynamically adjusts feature representations using a small dataset of real synthetic content, thereby enhancing model robustness. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MD-CSDNetwork significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in deepfake identification.

We establish a cluster type formulation for the classical Poisson structure on the classical limit of various quantized Borel subgroups within the context of quantized enveloping algebras. For quantized classical groups, we utilize cluster variables to define a family of non-rational functions possessing specific symmetry and recurrence characteristics. Leveraging these properties alongside the Kacy-Wakimoto representation, we demonstrate the Fock type characteristic nature of the corresponding quantum clusters. Furthermore, in the symmetry-breaking case, a similar demonstration applies to the standard quantum characteristic. Additionally, we introduce the standard quantum character and verify its cluster type nature through direct computation. Finally, in the symmetric case, the standard quantum character is identified with the cluster type function via its connection to the stochastic TASEP process.

This study examines Forsage, the world's largest multi-level marketing (MLM) fraud, which operated between 2019 and 2021. By analyzing Forsage's smart contract and associated blockchain data, along with an examination of the code developed by its creators, this research outlines the operational mechanics of the scheme, the logic behind its software, and the strategies employed to attract participants. Furthermore, the paper presents an ML-based model designed to forecast the system's collapse. This model aims to assist future stakeholders in identifying and evading similar MLM scams.

The identification of new clusters in the Galactic bulge holds significant importance for addressing key questions regarding globular cluster (GC) formation and evolution. Nevertheless, the bulge region remains a challenging environment for GC studies, as interstellar extinction obscures the area and high stellar density complicates the separation of genuine clusters from the background population. Leveraging the full dataset of the VVV survey, we conducted a detailed analysis of 19 candidate GCs located in the GC density ridge of the Galactic bulge. Although several of these candidates were previously noted in the literature, most lacked thorough examination. Our findings reveal that the sample's half-light radii range from 2.7 to 5.6 parsecs, while tidal radii extend between 15 and 30 parsecs. Regarding stellar populations, the sample exhibits classic GC characteristics, including a two-component structure in the color-magnitude diagram and a narrow distribution in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Furthermore, the sample's specific stellar density is comparable to that of typical Galactic globular clusters. While the sample's metallicities align with the mean of the Galactic GC population, they display a dispersion approximately twice as wide as usual. Finally, we determined the membership probabilities for individual stars within each cluster, concluding that these objects qualify as genuine globular clusters.

Deep-learning approaches hold significant potential for the prediction and analysis of business process performance. This study offers a comparative evaluation of various deep-learning models, contrasting them with traditional statistical and machine-learning methods. The evaluation framework employs real-world data from a genuine business environment, utilizing standard predictive metrics alongside process-discovery evaluation indicators. Our findings reveal that while deep-learning methods generally outperform traditional statistics and machine-learning counterparts in this context, the specific architectural design of the network plays a more critical role in performance than the choice of algorithm alone. Additionally, we introduce a novel application for standard word-embedding techniques within business process mining and identify a new metric specifically tailored for evaluating temporal predictions in business processes.

Reconstructing stellar spectra in the near-UV range offers a valuable tool for analyzing stellar atmospheres, particularly when dealing with objects where traditional photometric methods are constrained. This benefit was highlighted during the investigation of the solar transition region following the 1985 April 12 C2.2f event on AD Leo. Although the near-UV continuum could not be directly observed for this specific flare, its intense visible and infrared output enabled the derivation of relative fluxes across various visible and near-UV continuum bands by anchoring them to the spectral energy distribution (SED). Consequently, the flare's characteristics were simulated using HYST, a hydrostatic and time-dependent radiative transfer code. The model results successfully matched the observed visible and inferred SED data points, confirming the validity of the approach. Furthermore, the analysis of the near-UV continuum ratios derived from these matches provided critical constraints on the electron density and temperature structures within the flare's chromosphere.

Semantic-rich geometric models, including those built with triangles or point clouds, are frequently preferred over parametric representations like NURBS surfaces because they more intuitively convey functional details. Nevertheless, a significant hurdle in automatically generating such models lies in the multiple possible triangulations or reconfigurations a single manifold can exhibit. Although recent progress has successfully reduced the creation of "sliver" triangles—narrow elements that cause rendering issues and degrade deformation performance—it often fails to address the uniqueness of the result. Our work introduces the Transformant Point Cloud (TPC), a novel class of shared-skin animation for triangular meshed objects that incorporates stored transformation-invariant smoothing constraints. We further propose the Technique for Transformant Point Cloud (T3C), a streamlined workflow that streamlines the conversion of standard geometric formats into this new structure. T3C begins by generating an initial triangulation of a target model, followed by the sampling of millions of random viewpoints to capture multi-view smoothing constraints. These data points guide a guided mesh relaxation process that not only eliminates sliver triangles but also ensures surface smoothness. Subsequently, the refined mesh is parametrized onto a universal, unfolded UV layout, allowing associated texture maps and 3D geometry to be flattened into a single composite image. Finally, specific 2D video-based denoising techniques are applied directly to this UV-stitched texture to refine both the baked multi-view smoothing constraints and the original 3D asset simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach

The collective excitation of giant resonances significantly influences the synthesis of heavy elements. Within the RPA framework, a previously unobserved Jost function is employed to analyze electric quadrupole ($L=2$) and octupole ($L=3$) excitations across $p$-shell and $pn$-shell RPA models. For $p$-shell models, these calculations yield exact collective RPA eigenmodes, allowing precise identification of the real and imaginary components of the quadrupole and octupole electric polarizabilities. Regarding $pn$-shell models, the RPA diagonal Hamiltonian exhibits a structure that mirrors the separation of centers for independent single-particle states, resulting in collective modes with a real part strictly equal to zero energy and an imaginary part dependent on single-particle damping. Consequently, large damping induces a dissociation of these RPA collective modes. Specifically for $p$-shell $^{16}$O, this methodology successfully accounts for the complex GDO energy of $^{16}$O.

Dynamical systems modeling frequently depends on extensive empirical data, yet existing methods for assessing the relevance of data points typically treat variables as independent. This approach fails in many scenarios where data points exhibit correlations within specific dimensions. This paper introduces a novel impact-based clustering technique designed to categorize data points based on their influence on system dynamics, regardless of the underlying model structure. The method quantifies the distance between impacts before clustering, an metric that accounts for dependencies among features. Furthermore, it utilizes this metric to derive theoretical bounds for the region of attraction with a specified probabilistic guarantee, given a input dataset. The proposed impact-based clustering is then applied to weight data points in state-space identification processes for nonlinear dynamics, assigning higher significance to points with larger impacted areas. Finally, the utility of state-space impact clustering is demonstrated through numerical simulations and a real-world case study involving a robotic arm, highlighting its effectiveness in structural identification.

Although numerous models have demonstrated success in generating conversations, their efficacy often relies on diction complexity and grammatical accuracy that are impractical in dialogue scenarios where users speak casually. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework specifically designed for realistic multi-turn dialogue. Within this structure, we incorporate a discriminative agent that specifically evaluates whether generated responses appear authentic. Distinguishing ourselves further, we employ a sparse encoding strategy for the generator. By leveraging the high-classification capabilities of GANs alongside the parameter efficiency of sparse encoding, our approach effectively addresses the challenge of creating natural-sounding text. Because these models function as deep neural architectures, we also mitigate their tendency to overfit through a generator designed with a non-stationary optimisation process. Empirical results confirm that SparseGAN outperforms current state-of-the-art generation methods.

The concept of interstellar panspermia, wherein life transfers across stars via robust organisms or seeds capable of enduring harsh space conditions, remains a subject of debate in astrobiology. Although the extreme physical environment of the interstellar medium poses significant hurdles, the solar system's formation involved incorporating material from the wider galaxy, raising the possibility that biotic seeds were included. To assess the feasibility of detecting such panspermia during astronomical events, this study employs the standard model of interstellar passage to quantify survival rates against key factors: exposure to intense ultraviolet radiation in the interstellar UV field, intense stellar radiation near host stars, and the thermal fluctuations within the dense molecular clouds of the solar nebula. Using this framework, we analyze several astrophysical scenarios to identify which would leave observable signatures if interstellar transfer of life occurred. Our assessment indicates that if interstellar panspermia occurred, it would likely manifest during Novae outbursts, the planetary formation stages surrounding T Tauri stars, and the cataclysmic outbursts associated with Type Ia and IIn supernovae. Specifically, we argue that the biotic signatures embedded within meteoritic inclusions found in the outbursts of IIn Type Ia supernovae offer the most promising avenue for detection. Finally, we detail the specific parameters of a prototypical IIn Type Ia event that would impact micrometeoroids carrying potential seeds of life.

Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models are extensively utilized to estimate animal population sizes and density by incorporating location information into individual detection processes. Recently, a SCR framework that integrates non-spatial resource use data was introduced; however, because resources often vary significantly in their spatial arrangement, existing models may require refinement to account for the geographic context of utilization. This study proposes several models that integrate individual detection probabilities with both location and resource-use information. We demonstrate that these suggestions function as an extension of the standard SCR model, offering a distinct advantage over previous approaches by explicitly representing the spatial distribution of resources. We assess the properties of these proposed models through simulation analysis and apply them in a field test using wild elephants in Sri Lanka. The simulation results indicate that the integrated model accurately estimates population size, density, and individual detection probabilities. Furthermore, the application of the model to elephant data revealed that density estimates were enhanced by the inclusion of individual location and resource-use information, and the three different model specifications yielded largely consistent results.

Multilayer networks, where nodes connect across multiple distinct layers, are prevalent in both biological and technological domains. A significant challenge involves understanding how complex dynamical behaviors emerge from these inter-layer interactions. This study introduces a model of coupled Kuramoto oscillators designed to investigate the transmission of synchronized states through a multilayer structure. The chosen link weights are intentionally kept sub-critical to ensure that only one node achieves full synchronization amplitude, with its strength dictated entirely by the configuration of inter-layer connections. We demonstrate that even a minor modification in these cross-layer weights can cause a sudden inversion in which node becomes synchronized and a realignment of its amplitude. Such transitions are found to be governed by changes in the topological nature of the solution. Furthermore, the model reveals a strong correlation between the specific pattern of full-synchronization weight and the nodes' degree centrality within the network.

The classical theory of finite elasticity typically models the stress tensor $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ as a function of the deformation gradient $\mathbf{F}$, written $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{B})$, where $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{V}^{-2}$ is the left Cauchy-Green tensor and $\mathbf{Q}$ is a tensor function. Although standard assumptions such as material objectivity, symmetry, and equipollence restrict this mapping, they fail to prevent over-parameterization. This paper introduces the novel assumption of *orthogonal invariance*, defined as $\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{C}^T) = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{Q})\mathbf{Q}^T$ for all proper orthogonal $\mathbf{Q}$. Under this framework, the stress is expressed $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = W'\mathbf{Q}$, where $W'$ depends solely on the principal values of $\mathbf{Q}$. This formulation eliminates superfluent variables, yielding the most efficient representation.

Formal verification techniques are employed to eliminate errors from software, yet they often prove impractical for large-scale projects due to complexity and costs. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel method called "Geometric Testing" designed to uncover defects in real-world scenarios. The core concept involves modeling the code's control flow graph (CFG) as a geometric shape, where each statement corresponds to a line segment. Testing is achieved by constructing execution paths that function like rays originating from an initial point; these rays reflect off the segments to ensure comprehensive coverage of the logic. A significant advantage of this geometric framework is its ability to validate complex conditional structures, such as if-then statements, by guaranteeing that every possible path segment is traversed. The method was implemented in Java and evaluated against standard test suites for open-source Apache projects, demonstrating that it identifies bugs not caught by the original manual tests developed by the respective authors.

This paper examines the task of network scale estimation within a distributed computing environment, specifically addressing the challenge of counting nodes in small-world topology while present malicious actors. The scale, or total node count, is partitioned into blocks of fixed size $b$, with each block maintaining internal awareness of its count and the addresses of all contained nodes. Estimators are deployed as independent processes that originate at random locations, unaware of the global scale, global topology, or their own number. These estimators aggregate data from multiple runs to derive an approximation of the scale with high probability.

Regarding the population of malicious nodes, we assume they constitute a fraction $\epsilon$ of the total population, capable of acting collusively and arbitrarily to disrupt operations. The analysis establishes that provided the fraction $\epsilon$ remains below $1/6$, the number of small-world processes is sufficient to accurately estimate the scale with high certainty. The paper further investigates the complexity of this estimation task and derives both lower and upper bounds for the global scale, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm achieves a logarithmic complexity relative to the scale, or equivalently, a logarithmic complexity relative to the total number of nodes.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states, a challenge that can be met nonparametrically with recent advances in probe data technology. This study introduces new combinatorial formulas to derive short-term queue length distributions near road closures, relying exclusively on data from probe vehicles. By linking the numbers of probes exiting a saturated intersection or freeway merge/divide point to the underlying queue length, the method accounts for various possible departure patterns. Feasibility and application were demonstrated at a closed intersection in Los Angeles and a freeway bottleneck in Dallas.

Numerical simulations of gravitational fields, such as black hole mergers, face significant hurdles due to the initial data constraints inherent in Einstein's field equations. These nonlinear, second-order, coupled constraints are typically solved using iterative numerical techniques. A primary obstacle with these approaches is that they are often ill-posed, causing convergence issues or a lack of convergence to the correct solution. We propose a new strategy based on the Helmholtz decomposition that reformulates the constraints as a well-posed problem solvable via standard multigrid methods. Testing this technique on a known analytic solution for black hole initial data revealed that our approach not only achieves high accuracy but also converges geometrically with second-order multigrid.

The search for colossal positive Nernst effects in magnetic materials serves a dual purpose: it offers a promising pathway for developing efficient, temperature-insensitive magnetic sensors and provides profound insights into the exotic physics underlying the quantum anomalous Hall effect. In this study, we observe a massive positive Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN thin films, characterized by values reaching approximately $120 \, \mu\text{V}/\text{K}\cdot\text{T}$ near the antiferromagnetic transition temperature of 250 K. This observed magnitude is roughly three times greater than what can be predicted from the Seebeck and Hall coefficients, a discrepancy likely attributed to extreme transverse resistivity anisotropy driven by the materials' antiferromagnetic structure. Driven by this finding, we propose that the giant Nernst effect arises from the transverse resistivity anisotropy, prompting us to suggest a specific model for its explanation. Furthermore, we suggest that similar mechanisms responsible for this phenomenon may exist within other multiferroic or QAE-exhibiting magnetic materials.

Imagining intelligent machines capable of autonomous decision-making represents a transformative vision for scientific instrumentation. Although complete automation remains a long-term objective, integrating machine learning and data-driven techniques into daily operations can immediately enhance efficiency and effectiveness. This approach is particularly advantageous when dealing with complex systems involving high-throughput sample screening, multi-variable optimization, or large datasets. Furthermore, machine learning enables the maintenance of remote and sanitized experimental environments, which is critical for next-generation facilities designed for contactless, safe operations.

We examine the issue of isoperimetric residuals in $\mathbb{R}^n$, specifically the behavior of differences between $\mathbb{R}^n$'s volume and the volumes of two related regions derived from a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ possessing an approximately planar boundary. This approximation holds under the condition that hypersurfaces within it maintain bounded mean curvature. Our analysis indicates the existence of a characteristic length scale $\ell$, dependent on the parameters defining the domain $\Omega$ and its geometry, such that when this parameter approaches zero, there exists a rigid motion $\Phi_\ell$ and a translation vector $b_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^n$. These ensure $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges to the plane as $\ell \to 0$. Furthermore, we establish that $\mathbb{R}^n$ scales quadratically with respect to these parameters quadratic in $\ell$. We term this quadratic scaling a "smoothness criterion of scale $\ell$" and investigate its implications, demonstrating how it can be employed to refine criteria for the smoothness of embeddedness.

Fiber-reinforced polymer composites are increasingly utilized in structural health monitoring, yet damage detection often relies on empirical models that struggle to account for the complexity of damage propagation. This study introduces a novel self-sensing composite material designed for precise damage characterization through Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) and Genetic Algorithms (GAs). The proposed approach employs a Gaussian Process (EP) model to map EIT visualizations to damage states, leveraging data from controlled impact tests to establish a robust initial framework. Subsequently, GAs refine this model by optimizing weighting parameters for specific damage types, enabling more accurate detection strategies. Results demonstrate that this combined method significantly outperforms standard EIT results and raw visualizations in characterizing damage. Finally, the refined model was validated in real-time using an active damage introduction test, confirming its practical efficacy.

This paper is a conceptual exploration into the relationship between the cognitive capabilities of constituent parts and the system-wide intelligence, arguing that inverse proportionality often governs this dynamic. It examines diverse frameworks, including biological evolution, collective animal behaviors, human organizational structures, and artificial systems. The work formally introduces the "Law of Inverse Proportionality of Component and Systemic Intelligence" and investigates the "Paradox of Ascendant Particulate Wisdom." Ultimately, it offers a theoretical framework explaining how limited individual cognition can drive the emergence of profound collective intelligence.

A fundamental characteristic of a Euclidean space is the scalar product operation defined on its vectors, which adheres to specific axioms. While the theory of linear operators within this framework can be developed independently of an orthonormal basis, the present work establishes the corresponding model for tensors in Euclidean space using this same basis-dependent approach. As a result, the abstract character of the Euclidean structure remains integrated throughout the tensor description, explicitly manifesting as conditions of symmetry and positivity-definiteness. The explicit use of these geometric properties facilitates the construction of the Euclidean space theory of tensors and yields more streamlined formulations compared to conventional methods. The primary advantages derived from emphasizing this geometric aspect include a refined and simplified exposition of the Euclidean space theory of tensors, and the demonstration that the standard framework can be established entirely through vector concepts alone, devoid of any explicit reference to the underlying linear algebra of matrices.

We examine a model featuring a new $U(1)$ symmetry that is not conserved due to symmetry breaking, which suppresses interactions between charged particles and photons. This mechanism ensures that otherwise short-lived exotic particles acquire sufficient lifespans to traverse detector volumes before decaying. By extending the framework with quark mixing and flavor-violating couplings, we predict the production of neutral, metastable particles that decay into unflavored light particles. These particles are uniquely identifiable because they lack an electric dipole moment, causing trajectories to curve differently in magnetic fields compared to standard charged particles. We analyze the experimental signatures of these particles, demonstrating their potential detectability at the LHCb experiment.

Although brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) utilizing electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals have already enabled individuals to control computer cursors and computerized limbs, significant hurdles remain regarding the reliable generation of natural movements via BCIs. This research demonstrates that high-quality, high-gamma frequency (HGF) HGF ECoG signals, filtered for specific frequency ranges, contain sufficient information to decode walking states and accurately determine walking step rates. Specifically, a single-step Fourier method was applied to decode step rates from HGF ECoG data collected from two healthy participants walking on a treadmill. The resulting step rate estimates were cross-validated visually against actual steps, as well as quantitatively through power spectral density plots and scatter matrices. The resulting cross-validated correlation coefficients were found to be 0.98 for one subject and 0.99 for the other, with root-mean-square errors of 0.01 and 0.02 steps per minute, respectively. These findings suggest that HGF ECoG signals can decode walking states and step rates with exceptional accuracy, thereby offering a robust foundational step for developing a walking-capable BCI system.

If $G$ denotes a free abelian group of rank $n$ and $\mathcal{A}(G)$ represents the associated Artin action, we demonstrate that every splittings of the space $\mathbb{C}n$ relative to this action falls into one of two categories: either the line functions as an extreme ray within the first octant of $\mathbb{R}^n$, or it constitutes the diagonal of a 2-torus also acted upon by $G$.

Connecting the components of a system through effective connectivity analysis is crucial for understanding complex systems like the human brain. Traditional methods for estimating connectivity, however, often rely on linear or sparse assumptions that may fail to capture non-linear and rich interactive patterns, potentially leading to misleading inferences. Furthermore, existing non-linear techniques are computationally expensive, creating significant bottlenecks when analyzing large-scale systems. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce D3ECN, a deep network model designed to dynamic connectivity estimation. Benefiting from a residual-inception architecture, D3ECN adeptly models inter-variable relationships, while an adaptive mechanism automatically adjusts the dimensionality of connectivity space to fit specific tasks. Evaluations using both synthetic data and real fMRI datasets demonstrate that D3ECN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in performance and connects well with empirical observations. Crucially, compared to existing non-linear approaches, D3ECN achieves comparable accuracy with roughly a 90-fold improvement in efficiency.

The identification and characterization of biological motion within visual stimuli has long fascinated psychologists, neuroscientists, and computer vision experts. Biological motion, best exemplified by a walking person seen from behind, offers a compelling and efficient paradigm for studying how humans process dynamic scenes. This capability serves as a robust model system for investigating human psychology and neuroscience, as well as demonstrating a promising application in advanced visual tracking systems.

We introduce an innovative application of a recently developed technique for rapid approximate matrix inversion on GPU architectures, enhancing it through generalization. Adapting this approach to handle multiple right-hand sides and larger matrices, we ensure compatibility with current GPU constraints regarding constant memory usage. Furthermore, we extend the methodology to support numerically challenging sparse matrices containing negative or complex entries. Testing across various numerical simulations from GPU-accelerated physics and cosmology software packages highlights the approach's efficiency, versatility, and ease of integration.

The search for novel forms of Anderson localization, including scenarios where coexistence with topological order yields conductive modes, remains highly significant. In this study, we identify a Topological Anderson Insulator (TAI)—characterized by a non-zero conductance $G_{c}$—embedded within the integer quantum Hall regime (IQH), situated at the interface of two infinite sheets with opposite quantum Hall effects defined by distinct integer values of $|\nu|$. This topological insulation emerges specifically due to random binary disorder applied to the system. Notably, the resulting TAI exhibits a distinct property: $\nu$ flips its sign when the disorder randomness alters the resistivity from higher to lower values. Crucially, this topological conductivity does not rely on symmetry protection against backscattering, nor is it constrained by the specific nature of the disorder beyond being binary and random. Instead, it stems from a shift in the eigenstate localization properties of the initial quantum Hall states induced by such disordered conditions.

We analyze the scalar sector within the MSSM featuring complex parameters, which allows for three physical Higgs bosons and multiple mixing angles and mass terms. We derive explicit, complete formulas for scattering and decay processes of these particles, suitable for both LHC and future colliders. These details enable the construction of elaborate phenomenological scenarios, such as decay chains where a heavy on-shell Higgs splits into lighter Higgses that decay at the LHC, or the production of heavy Higgs pairs via boson fusion. Such phenomena are particularly relevant in regions of the parameter space characterized by large $\tan\beta$, large trilinear couplings, and tachyonic right-handed squarks, where heavy Higgs states can become accessible and phenomenologically significant.

We examine a distributed contextual linear bandit framework designed for large-scale applications, where the data volume is so extensive that a single learning agent cannot handle all training data at once. In this model, the agent partitions the dataset across multiple machines, pulling actions and receiving feedback locally, while each node transmits only condensed statistics to the agent. Distinct from prior work, our setting requires the individual agents to possess their own contextual stationary reward distributions; consequently, the optimal action varying by data subset means there is no single globally constant best choice. Acting within this intrinsic decentralized structure, we introduce a novel contextual algorithm that converges to the globally optimal arm with high probability. Furthermore, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound matching the scheme's complexity regarding both sample count and contextual information volume. Our findings surpass existing methodologies by offering a tight bound in a truly distributed paradigm and highlighting a key trade-off: enhanced statistical efficiency comes at the cost of assuming a stationary distribution at each location.

We present an investigation into the interplay between event shape characteristics and particle particle spectra, specifically analyzing their joint distributions in Pb-Pbe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}=2.76$ TeV. The study focuses on the dependence of particle yields on event shape engineering bins defined by transverse momentum broadening and flow squared ($v_2^2$). Our results indicate that incorporating event shape information significantly refines the description of elliptic flow ($v_2$) as a function of transverse momentum, particularly in the region dominated by the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) coupled system. Specifically, the model achieves superior accuracy for transverse momenta below approximately 1 GeV/c.
